topics.subject: Chemistry
topics.title: Excited Electrons
topics.description: Electrons that have absorbed energy and moved to a higher energy level than their ground state, and their return to lower energy levels.
learning_objectives: Explain how an electron becomes excited
Describe what happens when an excited electron returns to a lower energy level
Relate electron excitation to observable phenomena such as flame tests
topics.explanation: An electron becomes excited when it absorbs energy (for example from heat, electricity, or light) and moves from its normal, lowest-energy position (ground state) to a higher, unoccupied energy level. This excited state is unstable and temporary: the electron rapidly falls back down to a lower energy level (often directly back to the ground state, or via intermediate levels), releasing the absorbed energy as a photon of electromagnetic radiation, often as visible light. The exact frequency (and therefore colour, if visible) of the emitted light corresponds precisely to the energy difference between the excited level and the level the electron falls back to, which is unique for each element — this is the basis of flame tests and atomic emission spectra.
key_concepts: Emission of light on return to lower levels
Link to flame tests and spectra

definitions.definition: An electron that has absorbed energy and moved from its ground state to a higher, unoccupied energy level.

worked_examples.problem: Explain, in terms of excited electrons, why a sodium compound produces a yellow-orange flame when heated in a Bunsen flame.
worked_examples.working: Heat energy from the flame excites outer electrons in sodium atoms to higher energy levels. These excited electrons are unstable and quickly fall back to lower energy levels, releasing the absorbed energy as light.
worked_examples.answer: The energy released corresponds to a frequency of light in the yellow-orange part of the visible spectrum, characteristic of sodium, producing the observed flame colour.

practical_applications: Flame tests to identify metal ions
Fireworks, which use different metal compounds to produce different excited-electron flame colours
laboratory_applications: Carrying out flame tests: dipping a clean nichrome wire loop in a metal salt and holding it in a blue Bunsen flame, observing the characteristic colour produced as excited electrons return to lower energy levels
common_mistakes: Believing the electron stays permanently excited after gaining energy — excited states are always temporary and unstable
misconceptions: Assuming any energy input produces the same colour of light regardless of element — the specific colour depends on the unique energy level spacing of each element's electrons
tips: Link excitation directly to two key ideas: energy IN (absorption) moves an electron UP; energy OUT (emission, as light) happens as the electron falls back DOWN

basic.question: What happens to an electron's energy level when it absorbs energy?
basic.answer: It moves to a higher, excited energy level.

basic.question: What is released when an excited electron falls back to a lower energy level?
basic.answer: A photon of light (electromagnetic radiation) with energy equal to the difference between the two levels.

intermediate.question: Explain why flame tests can be used to identify different metal ions.
intermediate.answer: Each element has a unique arrangement of electron energy levels. When heated, electrons are excited and then fall back to lower energy levels, releasing light of specific frequencies determined by the exact energy gaps in that element. Because these energy gaps differ between elements, each metal produces a characteristic, identifiable flame colour.

advanced.question: Explain why an excited electron might emit several different frequencies of light as it returns to the ground state, rather than a single frequency.
advanced.answer: An excited electron does not always fall directly back to the ground state in a single step; it can fall through one or more intermediate energy levels before reaching the ground state. Each individual 'step' down between two energy levels releases a photon with energy (and therefore frequency) corresponding to that specific gap. If the electron takes a multi-step path, several different photons of different frequencies are released in total, which is why atomic emission spectra typically show multiple distinct lines rather than just one.

exam_style_questions.question: A student heats a compound in a Bunsen flame and observes a lilac flame colour, which she uses to identify the presence of potassium ions. Explain, in terms of electrons, how this flame colour is produced.
exam_style_questions.model_answer: Heat energy from the flame is absorbed by electrons in the potassium ions, promoting them from their ground state to higher, excited energy levels (1 mark). These excited states are unstable, so the electrons quickly fall back down to lower energy levels (1 mark). As they do so, they release the absorbed energy as light of a specific frequency (in the lilac/violet part of the spectrum), characteristic of potassium's unique electron energy level spacing (1 mark).

topics.summary: Excited electrons have absorbed energy and moved to a higher energy level; this state is unstable, and the electron returns to a lower level by emitting light of a specific frequency, characteristic of the element — the basis of flame tests and emission spectra.
revision_notes: Excitation: energy absorbed, electron moves up
Emission: electron falls back down, releases light
Frequency of light emitted is unique to each element
diagram_recommendations: [DIAGRAM: Electron transition diagram showing excitation (energy absorbed) and emission (photon released) between two energy levels]

topics.subject: Chemistry
topics.title: Atomic Emission Spectra
topics.description: The unique pattern of light frequencies emitted by excited atoms of an element as electrons fall back to lower energy levels, used to identify elements.
learning_objectives: Describe how an atomic emission spectrum is produced
Explain why each element produces a unique emission spectrum
Describe practical and scientific uses of emission spectra
topics.explanation: An atomic emission spectrum is produced when atoms of an element are given energy (e.g. by heating or an electric discharge), exciting electrons to higher energy levels; as these electrons fall back down to lower energy levels, they emit photons of light at specific frequencies corresponding exactly to the energy differences between levels. When this emitted light is passed through a prism or diffraction grating (in a spectroscope), it is split according to frequency, producing a series of distinct bright lines against a dark background — a line spectrum (see Line Spectra) — rather than a continuous rainbow of colour. Because every element has a unique set of electron energy levels, each element produces its own unique pattern of emission lines, which can be used to identify elements, including in stars and other astronomical objects far too distant to sample directly.
key_concepts: Excitation and emission produce the spectrum

definitions.definition: The unique pattern of specific light frequencies emitted by an element's excited atoms as electrons return to lower energy levels.

practical_applications: Identifying the elemental composition of stars and other astronomical objects from their emission (or absorption) spectra
Identifying unknown elements in a laboratory sample via their characteristic spectral lines
laboratory_applications: Observing simple flame test colours as a basic, visible example of atomic emission
Using a spectroscope to observe the detailed line spectrum of an element (e.g. hydrogen or helium in a discharge tube)
common_mistakes: Confusing an emission spectrum (produced by atoms releasing light) with an absorption spectrum (produced by atoms absorbing specific frequencies from a continuous light source passing through them, leaving dark lines)
misconceptions: Believing an atomic emission spectrum is a continuous band of all colours (a rainbow) — it consists of distinct, separate lines at specific frequencies only
tips: Remember: line spectra are direct evidence for the idea that electron energy levels are quantised (discrete), not continuous

basic.question: State what produces an atomic emission spectrum.
basic.answer: Excited electrons falling back to lower energy levels and emitting photons of specific frequencies.

basic.question: Describe the general appearance of an atomic emission spectrum.
basic.answer: A series of distinct, coloured (or otherwise specific-frequency) bright lines against a dark background, rather than a continuous range of colour.

intermediate.question: Explain why atomic emission spectra can be used to identify elements present in a distant star.
intermediate.answer: Each element produces a unique pattern of spectral lines, determined by its specific electron energy level structure. By analysing the pattern of lines present in light received from a star, scientists can match these lines to the known emission spectra of elements measured in laboratories on Earth, identifying which elements are present in the star, even though direct sampling is impossible.

advanced.question: Explain why an atomic emission spectrum consists of discrete lines rather than a continuous spectrum of all frequencies.
advanced.answer: Electrons within an atom can only occupy specific, quantised energy levels, not a continuous range of energies. When an excited electron falls to a lower energy level, the photon it emits has an energy (and therefore frequency, since photon energy is proportional to frequency) exactly equal to the specific gap between those two particular energy levels. Since only a limited, specific set of energy level gaps exist within any given atom, only a limited, specific set of photon frequencies can be emitted, producing distinct lines rather than a smooth, continuous range of all possible frequencies.

exam_style_questions.question: Explain why each element produces a unique atomic emission spectrum, and describe one practical use of this fact.
exam_style_questions.model_answer: Each element has a unique arrangement of electron energy levels, so the specific energy gaps between levels (and therefore the frequencies of light that can be emitted as excited electrons fall to lower levels) are different for every element (1 mark). This means the pattern of spectral lines produced acts like a unique 'fingerprint' for each element (1 mark). This can be used to identify unknown elements in a sample, or to determine the elements present in distant stars by analysing the light they emit (1 mark).

topics.summary: Atomic emission spectra are produced when excited electrons fall to lower energy levels, releasing light at specific frequencies unique to each element. This produces a line spectrum, used to identify elements in samples and in astronomical objects.
revision_notes: Emission spectrum: excited electrons fall down, release specific frequencies of light
Unique pattern of lines per element = fingerprint
Evidence for quantised (discrete) energy levels
diagram_recommendations: [DIAGRAM: Comparison of a continuous spectrum and a line emission spectrum for hydrogen]

topics.subject: Chemistry
topics.title: Line Spectra
topics.description: The pattern of discrete, separate lines seen in an atomic emission spectrum, providing direct evidence for quantised electron energy levels.
learning_objectives: Describe the appearance of a line spectrum
Explain what a line spectrum provides evidence for regarding electron structure
Relate line spacing/position to the arrangement of electron energy levels
topics.explanation: A line spectrum consists of a series of narrow, distinct, separate lines of specific colour (or, more generally, frequency) seen when the light emitted by excited atoms of an element is passed through a spectroscope, rather than a smooth, continuous band of all colours blending into each other. Each line corresponds to light released as an electron falls between two specific energy levels within the atom. The existence of line spectra (rather than continuous spectra) provided some of the earliest strong experimental evidence that electron energy levels within atoms are quantised — that is, electrons can only exist at specific, fixed energy values, not any value in between. The hydrogen atom's line spectrum, being the simplest atom with only one electron, was historically especially important in developing and testing early quantum models of the atom, including Bohr's model.
key_concepts: Each line = one specific electron transition

definitions.definition: A spectrum consisting of a series of narrow, discrete lines at specific frequencies, rather than a continuous range, produced by electron transitions between quantised energy levels.

practical_applications: Astronomical spectroscopy uses line spectra to determine the composition, and even motion (via the Doppler shift of spectral lines), of distant stars and galaxies
laboratory_applications: Viewing gas-discharge tubes (e.g. hydrogen or helium) through a spectroscope or diffraction grating to observe their characteristic line spectra directly
common_mistakes: Describing a line spectrum as 'a rainbow' — a rainbow is a continuous spectrum; a line spectrum has distinct gaps between separate lines
misconceptions: Believing line spectra are unique to only a few elements — every element produces its own unique line spectrum, since every element has a distinct electron energy level structure
tips: Remember the key link: continuous spectrum = all frequencies present (like white light through a prism); line spectrum = only specific frequencies present (from specific atomic electron transitions)

basic.question: Describe the appearance of a line spectrum.
basic.answer: A series of narrow, distinct, separate coloured lines against a dark background, rather than a continuous band of colour.

basic.question: What does each line in a line spectrum correspond to?
basic.answer: A specific electron transition between two particular energy levels within the atom, releasing a photon of a specific frequency.

intermediate.question: Explain why the observation of line spectra, rather than continuous spectra, supported the idea that electron energy levels are quantised.
intermediate.answer: If electrons could have any energy value at all (a continuous range), then transitions between energy states could in principle release photons of any frequency, producing a continuous spectrum with no gaps. The fact that only specific, distinct lines are observed shows that only specific, discrete photon energies (and therefore specific energy level gaps) are possible, which is only explicable if electrons themselves are restricted to specific, fixed (quantised) energy levels rather than a continuous range.

advanced.question: Explain why hydrogen's line spectrum was particularly important historically in developing the Bohr model of the atom.
advanced.answer: Hydrogen is the simplest atom, containing only a single electron and a single proton, making its energy level structure and resulting spectrum simpler to analyse mathematically than that of atoms with many electrons (where electron-electron interactions complicate the pattern). Bohr was able to use the precise, measured pattern and spacing of lines in hydrogen's spectrum to develop and test a mathematical model in which electrons occupy specific, fixed energy levels around the nucleus; the excellent agreement between his model's predictions and hydrogen's observed spectral lines provided strong supporting evidence for the idea of quantised electron energy levels.

exam_style_questions.question: Explain what a line spectrum is and why its existence provides evidence for quantised electron energy levels within atoms.
exam_style_questions.model_answer: A line spectrum consists of a series of narrow, discrete, separate lines at specific frequencies, rather than a continuous range of frequencies (1 mark). Each line corresponds to a photon released as an electron falls between two specific energy levels within an atom (1 mark). Since only certain specific frequencies (lines) are observed, rather than a continuous range, this shows that only certain specific energy level gaps exist within the atom — meaning electron energy levels must be restricted to fixed, discrete (quantised) values rather than being able to take any value (1 mark).

topics.summary: Line spectra consist of discrete lines at specific frequencies, each corresponding to a particular electron transition between energy levels. Their existence provided key evidence for quantised electron energy levels, historically important in developing atomic models such as Bohr's.
revision_notes: Line spectrum = discrete lines, not continuous
Each line = one specific electron energy transition
Key evidence for quantised (discrete) energy levels
related_topics: History of Atomic Theory (Dalton to Bohr)
diagram_recommendations: [DIAGRAM: Hydrogen's line spectrum in the visible region, showing distinct coloured lines]

topics.subject: Chemistry
topics.title: Ionisation Energy
topics.description: The energy required to remove one mole of electrons from one mole of gaseous atoms (or ions), and the periodic trends it shows.
learning_objectives: Define first ionisation energy
Explain the factors that affect ionisation energy
Describe and explain trends in ionisation energy across a period and down a group
topics.explanation: The first ionisation energy of an element is the energy required to remove one electron from each atom in one mole of gaseous atoms of that element, forming one mole of gaseous 1+ ions; it is always an endothermic process (energy must be put in to remove an electron against the attractive pull of the nucleus). Ionisation energy is affected by several factors: nuclear charge (more protons increase attraction on electrons, increasing ionisation energy), atomic radius (electrons further from the nucleus are less strongly attracted, decreasing ionisation energy), electron shielding (inner shell electrons repel and shield outer electrons from the full nuclear charge, decreasing ionisation energy), and, at a more detailed level, whether the electron being removed is from a full or half-full subshell, which can cause small irregularities in the general trend. Ionisation energy generally increases across a period (increasing nuclear charge, similar shielding, decreasing atomic radius) and decreases down a group (increasing atomic radius and shielding outweigh the increasing nuclear charge).
key_concepts: Factors: nuclear charge, atomic radius, shielding
Trends across periods and down groups

definitions.definition: The energy required to remove one electron from each atom in one mole of gaseous atoms of an element, forming one mole of gaseous 1+ ions.
The repulsive effect of inner-shell electrons on outer-shell electrons, reducing the attractive force felt from the nucleus.

equations: General first ionisation energy equation: X(g) → X+(g) + e−

worked_examples.problem: Write the equation representing the first ionisation energy of magnesium.
worked_examples.working: First ionisation energy always involves one mole of gaseous atoms losing one electron each to form gaseous 1+ ions, with all species in the gaseous state.

practical_applications: Ionisation energy trends help predict metallic character and reactivity across the periodic table, used in materials selection and understanding reactivity series
common_mistakes: Forgetting to include state symbols (g) for all species in ionisation energy equations — ionisation energy is defined specifically for gaseous atoms/ions
Confusing the trend directions: assuming ionisation energy increases down a group (it actually decreases, since atomic radius and shielding increase)
misconceptions: Believing ionisation energy always increases perfectly smoothly across a period without exception — small dips occur (e.g. between Groups 2 and 13, and between Groups 15 and 16) due to subshell stability effects
tips: Remember the general trend rule: ionisation energy increases across a period (left to right), and decreases down a group (top to bottom) — the opposite trend to atomic radius

basic.question: Define first ionisation energy.
basic.answer: The energy required to remove one electron from each atom in one mole of gaseous atoms of an element, forming one mole of gaseous 1+ ions.

basic.question: State whether ionisation energy is generally exothermic or endothermic.
basic.answer: Endothermic (energy must be supplied to remove an electron).

intermediate.question: Explain why ionisation energy generally increases across Period 3 (sodium to argon).
intermediate.answer: Across a period, nuclear charge increases (more protons) while electrons are added to the same outer shell, so shielding stays roughly constant. The increasing nuclear charge pulls the outer electrons in more strongly, and atomic radius decreases, both of which increase the energy required to remove an outer electron, so ionisation energy increases.

intermediate.question: Explain why ionisation energy decreases down Group 1 from lithium to caesium.
intermediate.answer: Down a group, atoms gain additional electron shells, increasing atomic radius and increasing electron shielding from inner shells. Both of these effects reduce the attractive force felt by the outer electron from the nucleus, outweighing the increase in nuclear charge, so less energy is needed to remove the outer electron, and ionisation energy decreases.

advanced.question: Explain why the first ionisation energy of boron (Group 13) is slightly lower than that of beryllium (Group 2), despite boron having a greater nuclear charge.
advanced.answer: Beryllium's outer electron configuration is 2s2, a filled s subshell, which is a relatively stable, lower-energy arrangement. Boron's outer electron configuration is 2s2 2p1, meaning its outermost electron is in a 2p orbital, which is at a slightly higher energy than the 2s orbital and also experiences some additional shielding from the 2s2 electrons. This makes boron's outermost electron easier to remove than would be predicted from nuclear charge alone, giving boron a slightly lower first ionisation energy than beryllium despite having one more proton.

exam_style_questions.question: Explain, in terms of nuclear charge, atomic radius and shielding, why the first ionisation energy of sodium is lower than that of chlorine, both in Period 3.
exam_style_questions.model_answer: Sodium has a smaller nuclear charge than chlorine (11 protons vs 17 protons) (1 mark). Sodium's outer electron is further from the nucleus (larger atomic radius) than chlorine's (1 mark), since atomic radius decreases across a period, and shielding from inner shells is broadly similar for both (1 mark). The combination of chlorine's greater nuclear charge and smaller atomic radius means its outer electrons are held more strongly, requiring more energy to remove, so chlorine has a higher first ionisation energy than sodium (1 mark).

topics.summary: First ionisation energy is the energy needed to remove one electron from each atom in a mole of gaseous atoms. It depends on nuclear charge, atomic radius and shielding, generally increasing across a period and decreasing down a group.
revision_notes: First IE: X(g) → X+(g) + e−, always endothermic
Increases across a period (more nuclear charge, smaller radius)
Decreases down a group (more shielding, larger radius)
Small irregularities: Group 2→13 dip, Group 15→16 dip
diagram_recommendations: [DIAGRAM: Graph of first ionisation energy against atomic number for Period 3 elements, showing the general increase and small dips]

topics.subject: Chemistry
topics.title: Successive Ionisation Energies
topics.description: The pattern of increasing energy required to remove each subsequent electron from an atom, used as evidence for shell structure.
learning_objectives: Define successive ionisation energy
Explain why successive ionisation energies always increase
Interpret large jumps in successive ionisation energy data as evidence for electron shell structure
topics.explanation: Successive ionisation energies are the energies required to remove each electron from an atom one at a time, in sequence: the first ionisation energy removes the first (outermost, least tightly held) electron, the second ionisation energy removes an electron from the resulting 1+ ion, and so on. Each successive ionisation energy is always greater than the one before, for two combined reasons: after each electron is removed, the ion has one fewer electron repelling the remaining ones (less electron-electron repulsion) while the same number of protons continues to attract them, so remaining electrons are held more tightly; additionally, once all the electrons in the outer shell have been removed, the next electron must come from a shell closer to the nucleus, which is far more strongly attracted, causing a very large jump in ionisation energy at that point. These large jumps in successive ionisation energy data provide strong experimental evidence for the existence of separate electron shells at different distances from the nucleus.
key_concepts: Large jumps indicate a new (inner) shell
Evidence for shell structure and group number

definitions.definition: The energy required to remove each electron from an atom or ion in turn, one at a time, forming ions of increasing positive charge.

equations: Second ionisation energy equation: X+(g) → X2+(g) + e−

worked_examples.problem: A large jump occurs between the 2nd and 3rd successive ionisation energies of an element. Suggest the number of electrons in the element's outer shell and its likely group.
worked_examples.working: A large jump after removing 2 electrons suggests the 3rd electron comes from a new, inner shell, meaning the outer shell contained only 2 electrons.
worked_examples.answer: The element likely has 2 outer-shell (valence) electrons, placing it in Group 2.

practical_applications: Successive ionisation energy data is used to determine an element's group and electron shell structure without needing to know its identity in advance
common_mistakes: Assuming successive ionisation energies increase by a constant, equal amount each time — they increase, but the increases become progressively larger, with especially large jumps between shells
misconceptions: Believing a large jump in successive ionisation energy data occurs randomly — it specifically occurs at the point where all outer-shell electrons have been removed and the next electron must come from a shell closer to the nucleus
tips: To find an element's number of outer-shell electrons (and therefore likely group) from a successive ionisation energy graph, count how many ionisation energies occur before the first big jump

basic.question: State whether successive ionisation energies of an atom generally increase or decrease.
basic.answer: They always increase.

basic.question: Write the equation for the third ionisation energy of an element X.

intermediate.question: Explain why successive ionisation energies of the same atom always increase.
intermediate.answer: As each electron is removed, the ion is left with fewer electrons but the same number of protons, so there is less electron-electron repulsion and the remaining electrons are attracted more strongly to the nucleus (or, equivalently, the ratio of protons to electrons increases, increasing the effective pull on each remaining electron), making each subsequent electron progressively harder, and therefore requiring more energy, to remove.

intermediate.question: A graph of successive ionisation energies for an element shows a very large jump between the 7th and 8th ionisation energies. Suggest the element's likely group.
intermediate.answer: Since the large jump occurs after 7 electrons have been removed, this suggests the element has 7 outer-shell (valence) electrons, placing it in Group 17 (the halogens).

advanced.question: Sketch (describe) the general shape of a successive ionisation energy graph for sodium (electron configuration 2,8,1), and explain the pattern of large jumps you would expect.
advanced.answer: The graph would show a relatively low first ionisation energy (removing sodium's single outer 3s electron), followed by a very large jump to a much higher second ionisation energy (since the next electron must be removed from the full, closer, more strongly attracted second shell). Ionisation energies 2 through 9 would then increase gradually (removing the 8 electrons of the second shell one at a time, each becoming progressively harder as electron-electron repulsion decreases with each removal), followed by another very large jump to the 10th ionisation energy (removing an electron from the innermost, first shell, held extremely tightly and closely to the nucleus). This pattern of one low value, then a big jump, then eight gradually increasing values, then another very large jump directly reflects sodium's 2,8,1 shell structure.

exam_style_questions.question: The first five successive ionisation energies of an element (in kJ/mol) are approximately 590, 1145, 4900, 6500, 8100, showing a large jump between the 2nd and 3rd values. Explain what this data suggests about the element's electron shell structure and likely group.
exam_style_questions.model_answer: The large jump between the 2nd and 3rd ionisation energies suggests that the first two electrons removed came from the same (outer) shell, while the third electron had to be removed from a shell much closer to the nucleus, requiring considerably more energy (1 mark). This suggests the element has 2 electrons in its outer shell (1 mark), placing it in Group 2 of the periodic table (this data corresponds to calcium) (1 mark).

topics.summary: Successive ionisation energies always increase as electrons are removed one at a time, due to decreasing electron-electron repulsion and, at shell boundaries, much larger jumps as an inner, more tightly-held shell is reached — providing direct evidence for electron shell structure and group number.
revision_notes: Successive IEs always increase
Large jump = start of removing electrons from the next (inner) shell
Number of IEs before first big jump = number of outer-shell electrons = group number (for main groups)
diagram_recommendations: [DIAGRAM: Graph of successive ionisation energies (log scale) for sodium, showing the shell-boundary jumps]

topics.subject: Chemistry
topics.title: Electron Affinity
topics.description: The energy change when one mole of electrons is added to one mole of gaseous atoms, forming gaseous 1- ions, and the trends this shows.
learning_objectives: Define first electron affinity
Explain why first electron affinity is usually exothermic while second electron affinity is endothermic
Describe the general trend in electron affinity across a period
topics.explanation: The first electron affinity of an element is the energy change when one electron is added to each atom in one mole of gaseous atoms, forming one mole of gaseous 1− ions. Unlike ionisation energy, first electron affinity is usually exothermic (energy is released), because the incoming electron is attracted to the positively charged nucleus, and this attraction outweighs the additional repulsion from existing electrons for most atoms. Second electron affinity (adding a further electron to an already negative ion, e.g. O−(g) + e− → O2−(g)) is always endothermic, since the incoming electron must be forced onto an already negatively charged ion, against strong electrostatic repulsion. Electron affinity generally becomes more exothermic (more negative) across a period (increasing nuclear charge and decreasing atomic radius increase attraction for an incoming electron), with the halogens (Group 17) showing particularly strongly exothermic first electron affinities, since gaining one electron gives them a stable, full outer shell.
key_concepts: Second (and further) electron affinity always endothermic
Halogens: strongly exothermic first electron affinity

definitions.definition: The energy change when one electron is added to each atom in one mole of gaseous atoms of an element, forming one mole of gaseous 1− ions.

equations: First electron affinity: X(g) + e− → X−(g)
Second electron affinity: X−(g) + e− → X2−(g)

worked_examples.problem: Explain why the second electron affinity of oxygen is endothermic, unlike its exothermic first electron affinity.
worked_examples.working: The first electron affinity adds an electron to a neutral atom, attracted by the nucleus. The second electron affinity adds an electron to an already negatively charged O− ion.
worked_examples.answer: The incoming electron in the second step is repelled by the existing negative charge on O−, requiring energy input to overcome this repulsion, making the second electron affinity endothermic.

practical_applications: Electron affinity values help explain and predict the formation and stability of ionic compounds, alongside lattice energy (see Ionic Bonding, Born-Haber Cycles)
common_mistakes: Assuming all electron affinities are exothermic like the first — only the first electron affinity is typically exothermic; subsequent ones are endothermic due to repulsion from the existing negative charge
misconceptions: Confusing electron affinity (an atom gaining an electron) with ionisation energy (an atom losing an electron) — they describe opposite processes with generally opposite typical signs (electron affinity usually exothermic; ionisation energy always endothermic)
tips: Remember: first electron affinity = usually exothermic (nucleus attracts new electron); any further electron affinity = always endothermic (repulsion from existing negative ion)

basic.question: Define first electron affinity.
basic.answer: The energy change when one electron is added to each atom in one mole of gaseous atoms of an element, forming one mole of gaseous 1− ions.

basic.question: State whether first electron affinity is usually exothermic or endothermic.
basic.answer: Usually exothermic.

intermediate.question: Write the equation for the first electron affinity of chlorine.
intermediate.answer: Cl(g) + e− → Cl−(g)

intermediate.question: Explain why fluorine has a strongly exothermic first electron affinity.
intermediate.answer: Fluorine has a small atomic radius and high nuclear charge relative to its shielding, so an incoming electron is strongly attracted to the nucleus. Gaining one electron also gives fluorine a full, stable outer shell (like the noble gas neon), both of which favour a large release of energy, giving fluorine a strongly exothermic first electron affinity.

advanced.question: Explain why the magnitude of first electron affinity generally increases (becomes more negative/exothermic) across Period 3, using both nuclear charge and atomic radius in your answer.
advanced.answer: Across Period 3, nuclear charge increases while shielding from inner-shell electrons stays broadly constant, and atomic radius decreases. Both effects increase the attractive pull the nucleus exerts on an incoming electron: increasing nuclear charge directly increases attraction, while decreasing atomic radius means the incoming electron is, on average, closer to the nucleus and therefore more strongly attracted. Together, these effects mean more energy is released as an electron is added, making the first electron affinity progressively more exothermic (more negative) across the period, though there are some irregularities related to subshell stability, similar to those seen in ionisation energy trends.

exam_style_questions.question: Explain why the first electron affinity of chlorine is exothermic, while its second electron affinity would be endothermic.
exam_style_questions.model_answer: In the first electron affinity, an electron is added to a neutral chlorine atom and is attracted by the positive nuclear charge, releasing energy overall, making the process exothermic (1 mark). In a hypothetical second electron affinity, a further electron would need to be added to an already negatively charged Cl− ion (1 mark). The incoming electron would be repelled by the existing negative charge on the ion, so energy must be supplied to overcome this repulsion, making the process endothermic (1 mark).

topics.summary: First electron affinity is the energy change when an atom gains an electron, usually exothermic due to nuclear attraction. Further electron affinities are always endothermic, due to repulsion from the ion's existing negative charge. Electron affinity generally becomes more exothermic across a period.
revision_notes: First EA: X(g) + e− → X−(g), usually exothermic
Second/further EA: always endothermic (repulsion from existing negative ion)
More exothermic across a period (more nuclear charge, smaller radius)

topics.subject: Chemistry
topics.title: Electronegativity
topics.description: A measure of the ability of an atom to attract the shared pair of electrons in a covalent bond, and the periodic trends it shows.
learning_objectives: Define electronegativity
Describe and explain trends in electronegativity across a period and down a group
Relate electronegativity difference to bond polarity
topics.explanation: Electronegativity is a measure of the ability of an atom, within a covalent bond, to attract the shared pair of bonding electrons towards itself. It is usually measured on the Pauling scale, with fluorine (the most electronegative element) assigned a value of about 4.0. Electronegativity depends on the same factors as ionisation energy: nuclear charge, atomic radius, and electron shielding. Electronegativity generally increases across a period (increasing nuclear charge, decreasing atomic radius, similar shielding, so bonding electrons are pulled more strongly) and decreases down a group (increasing atomic radius and shielding outweigh increasing nuclear charge, so bonding electrons further away are attracted less strongly). Noble gases are not usually assigned electronegativity values, since they rarely form covalent bonds. The difference in electronegativity between two bonded atoms determines bond polarity: a large difference gives a polar covalent bond (or, if large enough, an ionic bond); little or no difference gives a non-polar covalent bond.
key_concepts: Ability to attract shared bonding electrons
Trend across periods and down groups

definitions.definition: A measure of the ability of an atom in a covalent bond to attract the shared pair of bonding electrons towards itself.

worked_examples.problem: Explain whether the H-Cl bond is polar or non-polar, given that chlorine (electronegativity ≈3.0) is more electronegative than hydrogen (electronegativity ≈2.1).
worked_examples.working: Compare electronegativity values: chlorine attracts the shared electron pair more strongly than hydrogen, giving chlorine a partial negative charge and hydrogen a partial positive charge.
worked_examples.answer: The H-Cl bond is polar covalent, due to the electronegativity difference between H and Cl.

practical_applications: Electronegativity differences predict bond type (ionic, polar covalent, non-polar covalent) and molecular polarity, essential for predicting solubility, boiling points, and reactivity
common_mistakes: Confusing electronegativity (attraction for bonding electrons within a covalent bond) with electron affinity (energy change when a whole electron is gained by an isolated gaseous atom) — these are related but distinct concepts
misconceptions: Believing electronegativity only applies to ionic compounds — it is specifically a property relevant to covalent bonding, describing how bonding electrons are shared unequally
tips: Fluorine is the most electronegative element overall; electronegativity generally increases towards the top-right of the periodic table (excluding noble gases)

basic.question: Define electronegativity.
basic.answer: A measure of the ability of an atom in a covalent bond to attract the shared pair of bonding electrons towards itself.

basic.question: State which element has the highest electronegativity.
basic.answer: Fluorine

intermediate.question: Explain why electronegativity increases across Period 3 from sodium to chlorine.
intermediate.answer: Across the period, nuclear charge increases while shielding remains broadly constant and atomic radius decreases, so the nucleus exerts a stronger pull on the shared pair of bonding electrons in a covalent bond, increasing electronegativity.

intermediate.question: State the type of bond expected between two atoms of the same element, such as in Cl2, in terms of electronegativity difference.
intermediate.answer: A non-polar covalent bond, since both atoms have identical electronegativity, so there is no unequal attraction for the shared electron pair.

advanced.question: Explain, using electronegativity, why sodium chloride is considered an ionic compound while hydrogen chloride is considered a polar covalent compound, even though both involve a bond between two different elements.
advanced.answer: The electronegativity difference between sodium and chlorine is very large (sodium is a weakly electronegative metal, chlorine is strongly electronegative), large enough that chlorine effectively removes the bonding electron entirely from sodium, forming discrete Na+ and Cl− ions held together by electrostatic attraction — an ionic bond. The electronegativity difference between hydrogen and chlorine is smaller; while chlorine attracts the shared electron pair more strongly, giving the bond significant polarity (partial charges, δ+ on H and δ− on Cl), the electron pair is still meaningfully shared between both atoms rather than being fully transferred, characteristic of a polar covalent bond rather than a fully ionic one.

exam_style_questions.question: Explain why electronegativity decreases down Group 17 from fluorine to iodine.
exam_style_questions.model_answer: Down the group, atoms gain additional electron shells, increasing atomic radius (1 mark) and increasing electron shielding from inner-shell electrons (1 mark). Both of these effects reduce the attractive pull the nucleus can exert on a shared pair of bonding electrons in a covalent bond, outweighing the increase in nuclear charge, so electronegativity decreases down the group (1 mark).

topics.summary: Electronegativity measures an atom's ability to attract shared bonding electrons in a covalent bond, generally increasing across a period and decreasing down a group. Electronegativity differences between bonded atoms determine bond polarity, from non-polar covalent through polar covalent to ionic.
revision_notes: Electronegativity: attraction for shared bonding electrons (Pauling scale, F highest ≈4.0)
Increases across a period, decreases down a group
Difference in electronegativity → bond polarity (non-polar → polar covalent → ionic)

topics.subject: Chemistry
topics.title: Atomic Radius
topics.description: A measure of the size of an atom, and the periodic trends it shows across periods and down groups.
learning_objectives: Define atomic radius
Describe and explain the trend in atomic radius across a period and down a group
Explain how atomic radius is measured in practice
topics.explanation: Atomic radius is a measure of the size of an atom, generally taken as half the distance between the nuclei of two identical, adjacent, bonded atoms (since an atom's electron cloud does not have a sharply defined outer edge). Atomic radius decreases across a period, because nuclear charge increases while electrons are added to the same outer shell (so shielding stays roughly constant), meaning the increasing positive charge pulls the existing electron shell in more tightly. Atomic radius increases down a group, because each successive element has an additional electron shell, and although nuclear charge also increases, the effect of adding a whole new outer shell (further from the nucleus) dominates, along with increased shielding from the additional inner shells.
key_concepts: Definition based on bonded atom distance
Nuclear charge and shielding as underlying causes

definitions.definition: A measure of the size of an atom, typically taken as half the distance between the nuclei of two identical, adjacent, bonded atoms.

practical_applications: Atomic radius trends help predict and explain reactivity, ionisation energy and metallic character across the periodic table
laboratory_applications: Atomic radii are typically determined experimentally using X-ray diffraction to measure the distances between atoms in crystal structures
common_mistakes: Assuming atomic radius increases across a period, in the same direction as atomic number — it actually decreases across a period due to increasing nuclear charge
misconceptions: Believing atoms have a precisely defined 'edge' or boundary — since electron probability extends outward without a sharp cutoff, atomic radius is defined by convention (e.g. half the internuclear distance in a bonded pair) rather than an absolute physical boundary
tips: Remember: atomic radius decreases across a period (more pull, same shell), increases down a group (new shell added) — this trend is the reverse of ionisation energy's general trend

basic.question: State how atomic radius changes across a period, from left to right.
basic.answer: It decreases.

basic.question: State how atomic radius changes down a group.
basic.answer: It increases.

intermediate.question: Explain why atomic radius decreases across Period 2 from lithium to fluorine.
intermediate.answer: Across the period, electrons are added to the same outer (second) shell, so shielding remains roughly constant, while nuclear charge (number of protons) increases. The stronger nuclear charge pulls the outer electron shell in more tightly towards the nucleus, without a corresponding increase in shielding to counteract this, so atomic radius decreases.

intermediate.question: Explain why atomic radius increases down Group 1 from lithium to potassium.
intermediate.answer: Down the group, each element has one additional electron shell compared to the one above it. Although nuclear charge also increases, the outer electron is in a shell that is both further from the nucleus and more strongly shielded by additional inner-shell electrons, so the overall effect is an increase in atomic radius, despite the greater nuclear charge.

advanced.question: Explain why the decrease in atomic radius across a period is generally smaller in magnitude than the increase in atomic radius down a group.
advanced.answer: Across a period, only the effective nuclear charge changes significantly (increasing) while electrons are added to the same shell, producing a relatively gradual and modest decrease in atomic radius as the electron cloud is drawn in slightly. Down a group, an entirely new outer shell is added at a significantly greater average distance from the nucleus, and the increased number of inner shielding shells substantially reduces the effective nuclear charge felt by the new outer electron; both of these effects compound to produce a comparatively large increase in atomic radius between successive elements down a group.

exam_style_questions.question: Explain why sodium has a larger atomic radius than chlorine, even though chlorine has a greater number of protons.
exam_style_questions.model_answer: Sodium and chlorine are both in Period 3 and have electrons in the same outer shell, but chlorine has a greater nuclear charge (more protons) than sodium (1 mark). Since shielding is broadly similar for both (same number of inner shells), chlorine's greater nuclear charge pulls its outer electron shell in more tightly than sodium's (1 mark), resulting in chlorine having a smaller atomic radius than sodium despite having more protons, because atomic radius across a period is dominated by the change in nuclear attraction on the same outer shell, not simply by the number of protons alone (1 mark).

topics.summary: Atomic radius, the size of an atom, decreases across a period (increasing nuclear charge on a constant shell) and increases down a group (additional shells and shielding outweigh increasing nuclear charge).
revision_notes: Atomic radius = half internuclear distance between bonded identical atoms
Decreases across a period; increases down a group
Reverse general trend to ionisation energy

topics.subject: Chemistry
topics.title: Ionic Radius
topics.description: A measure of the size of an ion, and how it compares to the atomic radius of the parent atom depending on whether electrons are lost or gained.
learning_objectives: Define ionic radius
Explain why cations are smaller than their parent atoms and anions are larger
Compare the relative sizes of isoelectronic ions
topics.explanation: Ionic radius is a measure of the size of an ion. When an atom loses one or more electrons to form a cation, the ionic radius is smaller than the atomic radius, because an entire outer shell of electrons may be removed (reducing the number of occupied shells), and because the remaining electrons experience a stronger net attraction from the unchanged nuclear charge acting on fewer electrons, pulling them in more closely. When an atom gains one or more electrons to form an anion, the ionic radius is larger than the atomic radius, because the increased number of electrons increases electron-electron repulsion, and the same nuclear charge is now shared among (and therefore attracts less strongly) more electrons, allowing the electron cloud to expand. For a series of ions with the same electron configuration (isoelectronic ions, e.g. Na+, Mg2+, Al3+, all with the neon configuration), ionic radius decreases as nuclear charge increases, since more protons pull the same number of electrons in more tightly.
key_concepts: Isoelectronic ions and nuclear charge effect

definitions.definition: A measure of the size of an ion, which differs from the atomic radius of the parent atom due to the loss or gain of electrons.
Describes atoms or ions that have identical electron configurations (the same number and arrangement of electrons).

worked_examples.problem: Explain why the ionic radius of Na+ is smaller than the atomic radius of a sodium atom.
worked_examples.working: A sodium atom (2,8,1) loses its single outer-shell electron to form Na+ (2,8), removing the outermost shell entirely and leaving fewer electrons attracted by the same nuclear charge.
worked_examples.answer: Na+ has one fewer occupied shell than the sodium atom, and its remaining electrons are pulled in more tightly by the unchanged nuclear charge, making Na+ significantly smaller than a sodium atom.

practical_applications: Ionic radius trends influence the structure and properties of ionic compounds, including lattice energy and solubility
common_mistakes: Assuming all ions are smaller than their parent atoms — this is only true for cations; anions are larger than their parent atoms
misconceptions: Believing ionic radius depends only on the number of electrons — for isoelectronic ions with the same number of electrons, ionic radius still varies because nuclear charge (number of protons) differs between them
tips: Remember: cations (positive, fewer electrons) = smaller; anions (negative, more electrons) = larger, compared to the parent atom

basic.question: State whether a cation is generally larger or smaller than its parent atom.
basic.answer: Smaller.

basic.question: State whether an anion is generally larger or smaller than its parent atom.
basic.answer: Larger.

intermediate.question: Explain why a chloride ion (Cl−) is larger than a chlorine atom.
intermediate.answer: The chloride ion has one more electron than the chlorine atom, but the same number of protons. This extra electron increases electron-electron repulsion within the ion, and the same nuclear charge must now attract one more electron, giving a slightly weaker average pull per electron, allowing the electron cloud to expand and making Cl− larger than a neutral Cl atom.

intermediate.question: Na+, Mg2+ and Al3+ are isoelectronic (all have the electron configuration 2,8). Explain why Al3+ has the smallest ionic radius of the three.
intermediate.answer: All three ions have exactly the same number of electrons (10) and the same electron configuration, but they have different nuclear charges: Al3+ has the greatest number of protons (13) compared to Mg2+ (12) and Na+ (11). Since the same number of electrons is attracted by an increasingly larger nuclear charge, the electron cloud is pulled in most strongly for Al3+, giving it the smallest ionic radius of the three isoelectronic ions.

advanced.question: Explain why the ionic radius of O2− is larger than that of F−, even though F has a greater atomic number (nuclear charge) than O.
advanced.answer: O2− and F− are isoelectronic, both having 10 electrons (the neon configuration). However, oxygen has fewer protons (8) than fluorine (9), so the nuclear charge attracting the same 10 electrons is smaller for O2− than for F−. With a weaker net nuclear attraction per electron, the electron cloud of O2− is held less tightly and can expand further than that of F−, giving O2− the larger ionic radius despite fluorine having the higher atomic number as a neutral atom.

exam_style_questions.question: Explain why a magnesium ion (Mg2+) has a smaller ionic radius than a magnesium atom.
exam_style_questions.model_answer: A magnesium atom loses its two outer-shell (3s) electrons to form Mg2+, removing the outermost occupied shell entirely (1 mark). This leaves Mg2+ with one fewer occupied electron shell than the neutral atom (1 mark). The remaining electrons are attracted by the same, unchanged nuclear charge but there are fewer of them, so they experience a stronger net attraction and are pulled in more closely to the nucleus, making Mg2+ considerably smaller than a magnesium atom (1 mark).

topics.summary: Ionic radius describes the size of an ion. Cations are smaller than their parent atom (fewer/removed shells, stronger net attraction); anions are larger (more electron-electron repulsion, weaker net attraction per electron). For isoelectronic ions, radius decreases as nuclear charge increases.
revision_notes: Cation < parent atom; Anion > parent atom
Isoelectronic ions: more protons = smaller radius
Same underlying cause as atomic radius trends: nuclear charge vs electron number/shielding

topics.subject: Chemistry
topics.title: Nuclear Charge
topics.description: The total positive charge of an atom's nucleus, determined by its number of protons, and its role in attracting electrons.
learning_objectives: Define nuclear charge
Explain the relationship between nuclear charge and atomic number
Explain how nuclear charge affects the attractive force on electrons
topics.explanation: Nuclear charge is the total positive electric charge of an atom's nucleus, resulting from the protons it contains; it is numerically equal to the atomic number of the element. A greater nuclear charge exerts a stronger electrostatic force of attraction on the surrounding electrons, all else being equal. Nuclear charge increases by one unit for each successive element across the periodic table (as atomic number increases by one), which is the fundamental underlying cause of many periodic trends, including the general decrease in atomic radius and increase in ionisation energy across a period. However, the effect actually experienced by outer electrons is better described by effective nuclear charge, which accounts for the shielding effect of inner-shell electrons (see Effective Nuclear Charge).
key_concepts: Nuclear charge = number of protons = atomic number
Stronger nuclear charge → stronger attraction on electrons
Underlying cause of many periodic trends

definitions.definition: The total positive electric charge of an atom's nucleus, equal to the number of protons (and therefore the atomic number).

practical_applications: Nuclear charge trends underpin the explanation of atomic radius, ionisation energy and electronegativity trends across the periodic table
common_mistakes: Confusing nuclear charge (the total charge, equal to atomic number) with effective nuclear charge (the net charge actually experienced by an outer electron, after accounting for shielding)
misconceptions: Believing nuclear charge alone determines atomic size or ionisation energy trends — shielding from inner electrons must also be considered, since it reduces the net attractive effect experienced by outer electrons
tips: Nuclear charge = atomic number, always; this is the simplest of the trend-related definitions to recall correctly

basic.question: Define nuclear charge.
basic.answer: The total positive electric charge of an atom's nucleus, equal to the number of protons.

basic.question: State the nuclear charge of an atom with atomic number 15.

intermediate.question: Explain why increasing nuclear charge across a period generally causes atomic radius to decrease.
intermediate.answer: As nuclear charge increases across a period while electrons are added to the same outer shell (so shielding stays roughly constant), the stronger positive charge exerts a greater attractive pull on the outer electrons, drawing the electron cloud in more closely to the nucleus and decreasing atomic radius.

advanced.question: Explain why nuclear charge alone is not sufficient to fully explain the trend in atomic radius down a group, and what additional factor must be considered.
advanced.answer: Although nuclear charge does increase down a group (more protons are added at each successive element), atomic radius actually increases down a group rather than decreasing, which nuclear charge alone would not predict. This is because each successive element down a group also gains an additional electron shell, and the shielding effect from these additional inner shells increases substantially, reducing the effective nuclear charge felt by the outer electrons. The combined effect of an additional shell (greater distance from the nucleus) and increased shielding outweighs the increase in nuclear charge, so atomic radius increases overall down a group, despite the higher nuclear charge.

exam_style_questions.question: State the relationship between nuclear charge and atomic number, and explain why nuclear charge alone does not fully determine the strength of attraction experienced by a particular outer electron.
exam_style_questions.model_answer: Nuclear charge is numerically equal to atomic number, since both are determined by the number of protons in the nucleus (1 mark). However, the actual attractive force experienced by a specific outer electron is reduced by shielding from inner-shell electrons, which repel and partially cancel out the effect of the full nuclear charge (1 mark), so the net attraction is better described by effective nuclear charge, which takes shielding into account, rather than nuclear charge alone (1 mark).

topics.summary: Nuclear charge is the total positive charge of the nucleus, equal to atomic number, and underlies many periodic trends by determining the base level of attraction on electrons — though the full picture requires accounting for shielding via effective nuclear charge.
revision_notes: Nuclear charge = number of protons = atomic number
Greater nuclear charge = stronger attraction on electrons (before considering shielding)
Distinct from effective nuclear charge, which accounts for shielding

topics.subject: Chemistry
topics.title: Effective Nuclear Charge
topics.description: The net positive charge actually experienced by an electron in an atom, after accounting for the shielding effect of other electrons.
learning_objectives: Define effective nuclear charge
Explain how shielding reduces effective nuclear charge below the full nuclear charge
Use effective nuclear charge to explain periodic trends more precisely than nuclear charge alone
topics.explanation: Effective nuclear charge is the net positive charge that a particular electron actually experiences, after taking into account the shielding (screening) effect of other electrons, particularly those in inner shells, which repel outer electrons and partially cancel out the full attractive pull of the nucleus. Effective nuclear charge is always less than the full nuclear charge (equal to atomic number) for any electron beyond the first, because inner electrons shield outer electrons from the full nuclear attraction, while electrons within the same shell shield each other only slightly. Effective nuclear charge increases across a period (since shielding from electrons in the same outer shell is relatively weak, so the increasing nuclear charge is felt more strongly), which more precisely explains the decrease in atomic radius and increase in ionisation energy seen across a period, compared to using nuclear charge alone.
key_concepts: Net charge felt by an electron, accounting for shielding
Always less than full nuclear charge
More precise explanation of periodic trends than nuclear charge alone

definitions.definition: The net positive charge experienced by a given electron in an atom, equal to the full nuclear charge reduced by the shielding effect of other electrons.

formulae.name: Simplified effective nuclear charge
formulae.formula: effective nuclear charge ≈ number of protons − number of shielding (inner) electrons
formulae.description: A simplified estimate; more detailed calculations (e.g. Slater's rules) refine this further, but are beyond introductory level.

worked_examples.problem: Estimate the effective nuclear charge experienced by an outer-shell electron in a sodium atom (atomic number 11, configuration 2,8,1), using the simplified approximation that inner-shell electrons fully shield outer electrons.
worked_examples.working: Sodium has 11 protons. Its outer (3rd shell) electron is shielded by the 10 inner electrons (2 in shell 1, 8 in shell 2).

practical_applications: Effective nuclear charge provides a more accurate model for predicting and explaining detailed periodic trends in atomic radius, ionisation energy and electronegativity
common_mistakes: Assuming electrons in the same shell provide the same amount of shielding as electrons in inner shells — electrons in the same outer shell shield each other only weakly, which is why effective nuclear charge still increases noticeably across a period
misconceptions: Believing effective nuclear charge stays constant across a period, since 'shielding is happening' — while total nuclear charge and total electron count both increase together across a period, the extra electrons are added to the *same* outer shell (weak mutual shielding), so effective nuclear charge on that shell still increases overall
tips: Use the simplified rule as an estimate: effective nuclear charge ≈ number of protons − number of electrons in complete inner shells (ignoring weaker same-shell shielding for a first approximation)

basic.question: Define effective nuclear charge.
basic.answer: The net positive charge experienced by a given electron in an atom, after accounting for the shielding effect of other electrons.

basic.question: State whether effective nuclear charge is generally greater than, less than, or equal to the full nuclear charge.
basic.answer: Less than (for any electron beyond the innermost).

intermediate.question: Estimate the effective nuclear charge on an outer electron in a magnesium atom (12 protons, configuration 2,8,2), using the simplified shielding approximation.
intermediate.answer: Effective nuclear charge ≈ 12 protons − 10 inner shielding electrons = approximately +2.

intermediate.question: Explain why effective nuclear charge increases across Period 3, even though shielding is present throughout.
intermediate.answer: Across Period 3, electrons are added to the same outer (third) shell, and electrons within the same shell shield each other only weakly compared to inner-shell electrons. Since the number of protons (and therefore full nuclear charge) increases with each element, while the shielding from inner shells (shells 1 and 2) stays constant, the effective nuclear charge experienced by the outer shell increases steadily across the period.

advanced.question: Explain why effective nuclear charge provides a better explanation than nuclear charge alone for why atomic radius decreases across a period but increases down a group.
advanced.answer: Nuclear charge (equal to atomic number) increases in both directions — across a period and down a group — so nuclear charge alone cannot explain why atomic radius changes in opposite directions in these two cases. Effective nuclear charge accounts for shielding, which behaves very differently in each direction: across a period, shielding from same-shell electrons is weak and roughly constant, so effective nuclear charge rises steadily, pulling the electron cloud in and decreasing radius. Down a group, each new element gains an entire additional inner shell, providing much stronger shielding that increases substantially alongside nuclear charge; this stronger shielding, combined with the new, more distant outer shell, means effective nuclear charge on the outermost electron does not increase as sharply (and the added shell distance dominates), so atomic radius increases down a group despite nuclear charge also increasing.

exam_style_questions.question: Explain the difference between nuclear charge and effective nuclear charge, and state which one increases across a period due to weak same-shell shielding.
exam_style_questions.model_answer: Nuclear charge is the total positive charge of the nucleus, determined simply by the number of protons (equal to atomic number) (1 mark). Effective nuclear charge is the net charge actually experienced by a specific electron, after accounting for the shielding effect of other electrons, and is always lower than the full nuclear charge (1 mark). Effective nuclear charge increases across a period, because shielding between electrons in the same outer shell is relatively weak, so the increasing nuclear charge is felt more strongly by outer electrons as more protons are added (1 mark).

topics.summary: Effective nuclear charge is the net attractive charge an electron actually experiences after accounting for shielding by other electrons; it is always less than the full nuclear charge, and its increase across a period (due to weak same-shell shielding) more precisely explains trends in atomic radius and ionisation energy than nuclear charge alone.
revision_notes: Effective nuclear charge = full nuclear charge − shielding effect
Simplified estimate: protons − inner shielding electrons
Increases across a period (weak same-shell shielding); key to explaining periodic trends precisely

topics.subject: Chemistry
topics.title: Quantum Numbers
topics.description: The set of four numbers that together uniquely describe the state of each electron in an atom, including its shell, subshell, orbital orientation and spin.
learning_objectives: State the four quantum numbers and what each one describes
Explain how quantum numbers relate to shells, subshells and orbitals
Apply the Pauli exclusion principle in terms of quantum numbers
topics.explanation: Quantum numbers are a set of four numbers that together uniquely describe the state of every electron in an atom. The principal quantum number (n) describes the main shell (energy level) an electron occupies, taking positive whole-number values (1, 2, 3...) — larger n means a shell further from the nucleus and higher in energy. The azimuthal (angular momentum, or subshell) quantum number (l) describes the subshell/orbital shape within a shell, taking values from 0 to (n−1), corresponding to s (l=0), p (l=1), d (l=2), f (l=3) subshells. The magnetic quantum number (ml) describes the specific orbital's orientation in space within a subshell, taking integer values from −l to +l (e.g. for a p subshell, l=1, so ml can be −1, 0, or +1, corresponding to the three p orbitals). The spin quantum number (ms) describes the direction of an electron's intrinsic spin, taking one of only two values, commonly represented as +1/2 or −1/2. The Pauli exclusion principle can be restated precisely using quantum numbers: no two electrons in the same atom can have an identical set of all four quantum numbers.

definitions.definition: A positive whole number describing the main electron shell (energy level) an electron occupies.
A number, from 0 to (n−1), describing the subshell (shape) an electron occupies within its shell: 0=s, 1=p, 2=d, 3=f.
A number, from −l to +l, describing the specific orbital's orientation within a subshell.
A value of +1/2 or −1/2 describing the intrinsic spin direction of an electron.

worked_examples.problem: State the possible values of the azimuthal quantum number (l) for an electron in the third shell (n=3), and identify which subshells these correspond to.
worked_examples.working: l can take values from 0 to (n−1), so for n=3, l = 0, 1, or 2.
worked_examples.answer: l=0 (3s subshell), l=1 (3p subshell), l=2 (3d subshell)

practical_applications: Quantum numbers provide the fundamental theoretical basis for the entire structure of the periodic table and for predicting atomic spectra
common_mistakes: Confusing the azimuthal quantum number (l, describing subshell shape) with the principal quantum number (n, describing shell number)
Forgetting that l can only range from 0 to (n−1), not up to n
misconceptions: Believing quantum numbers are an entirely separate topic from shells, subshells and orbitals covered elsewhere — they are the precise mathematical description underlying those more familiar, simplified models
tips: Remember the mnemonic order and letters: n = shell number; l = subshell shape/type (0=s,1=p,2=d,3=f); ml = specific orbital orientation; ms = spin (±1/2)

basic.question: State what the principal quantum number (n) describes.
basic.answer: The main electron shell (energy level) an electron occupies.

basic.question: State the two possible values of the spin quantum number (ms).

intermediate.question: For an electron in a 2p orbital, state the value of the principal quantum number (n) and the azimuthal quantum number (l).
intermediate.answer: n = 2 (second shell); l = 1 (p subshell)

intermediate.question: Explain, using quantum numbers, why a p subshell contains exactly three orbitals.
intermediate.answer: For a p subshell, l=1, and the magnetic quantum number ml can take integer values from −l to +l, giving three possible values: −1, 0, and +1. Each distinct value of ml corresponds to a separate orbital with a different spatial orientation, so there are exactly three p orbitals within a p subshell.

advanced.question: State the Pauli exclusion principle in terms of quantum numbers, and use it to explain why an s subshell (with only one possible ml value) can still hold two electrons.
advanced.answer: The Pauli exclusion principle states that no two electrons within the same atom can have an identical set of all four quantum numbers (n, l, ml, ms). For an s subshell, l=0, and since ml can only take the value 0 (as it ranges from −l to +l, which for l=0 is just 0), there is only one s orbital. However, because two electrons in this one orbital can still differ in their spin quantum number (one +1/2, one −1/2), they have different, non-identical, complete sets of all four quantum numbers, so the Pauli exclusion principle allows up to two electrons (with opposite spins) to occupy the single s orbital.

exam_style_questions.question: State the four quantum numbers, what each one describes, and explain how they together specify the Pauli exclusion principle.
exam_style_questions.model_answer: Principal quantum number (n): describes the electron's main shell (1 mark). Azimuthal quantum number (l): describes the subshell/shape, from 0 to n−1 (1 mark). Magnetic quantum number (ml): describes the specific orbital's orientation, from −l to +l (1 mark). Spin quantum number (ms): describes electron spin direction, +1/2 or −1/2; the Pauli exclusion principle states that no two electrons in the same atom can share an identical set of all four of these quantum numbers (1 mark).

topics.summary: Four quantum numbers together uniquely describe every electron in an atom: principal (n, shell), azimuthal (l, subshell shape), magnetic (ml, orbital orientation), and spin (ms, spin direction). The Pauli exclusion principle states no two electrons can share an identical full set of these four numbers.
revision_notes: l = subshell (0 to n−1; 0=s,1=p,2=d,3=f)
ml = orbital orientation (−l to +l)
ms = spin (+1/2 or −1/2)
Pauli exclusion: no two electrons share all four identical values
